utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. For the record, all the accused are here. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. And from the Defence side, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes. Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes. Yes. Are there any preliminaries? None. So we proceed with your first witness, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon and welcome back. Our first witness will be Dr. Professor Slobodan Remetic, and I think we all have his report. We've also provided the booth with the report, both in B/C/S and in English, so that it may be easier for them to follow some of the linguistical terms that we may be using today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Professor. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I wonder is whether you know who's talking to you, because you're looking at the wrong direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it better. I will be speaking in English, and most of the proceedings today will be in English. You will be receiving interpretation simultaneously. If there are problems with interpretation, please let me know immediately. You've been summoned here as a witness by the Defence team of Ljubisa Beara. Before you start your testimony, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be speaking the truth, the text of which is being handed to you now. Please read that out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Ostojic will go first. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you know, my name is John Ostojic, and I will be asking you some questions here today, and hopefully we can finish today with at least my direct examination. Sir, can you, for the record, please state your full name for us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Remetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, I note from your CV and in other papers that you have written that you are a professor as well as a doctor. How would you like me to refer to you, as "Professor Remetic" or "Dr. Remetic"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: It doesn't really make any difference. You can just call me "Mr. Remetic." It's okay as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Remetic, before you, you have a set of documents, and just so that the record is clear, can you just share with us what those documents are?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I have received 18 intercepts from the Defence counsel representing Mr. Beara. I have also received a short curriculum vitae of Mr. Beara. I've also been provided with the statements of the operatives who allegedly recorded the intercepted conversations. I also have received the NIOD's criticism, i.e., their review of the work of the operatives. And I believe this is -- this sums up the most important things that I've had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Remetic, we'll go through your report in order to explain and expand on some of the items that you give opinions on, but I just needed to know: In front of you today, on the table that's before you, can you just tell us, do you have your report there dated the 18th of April, 2008? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have before me the text of the report that I submitted on the 18th of April to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear and our record is clear, it's 2D551 that reported the 18th of April, 2008. Also before you, sir, you referenced 18 intercepts. Do you have a packet of those 18 intercepts with you as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have the intercepts as well. They are right before me, next to the linguistic analysis of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll be going through that a little later in our discussion here this afternoon. I just wanted to know what you had in front of you. Now, let's talk about you, yourself, first. And can you give us a little background? When were you born and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of August, 1945, in the village of Kovacevici, municipality of Kladanj in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I completed elementary school and secondary school in Kladanj. I went to university in Novi Sad, and that's where I graduated from the School of South Slavonic Languages in 1970. I obtained my masters degree in Belgrade in 1976, and I obtained my doctoral degree at the Faculty of Philosophy in Novi Sad in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And can you share with us what your profession is currently?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Currently, I've been dealing with intercepts most of the time, but, generally speaking, I'm a professor at the School of Philosophy Nis, and I'm also part-time professor at the School of Philosophy in Banja Luka. I'm a member of the Academy of Sciences of Republika Srpska, and I'm in charge of a project there, and I'm also in charge of a project of the investigation of the dialect of the Serbian language, which is conducted by the Institute for the Serbian Language with the Serbian Academy of Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I note on page 3 of your report, 2D551, you list some of your other academic accomplishments, if you will. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. I am a member of several editorial boards. Actually, of the three editorial boards of the leading linguistic magazines in Belgrade, the Serbian Dialectological Magazine, the Onomatological Proceeds and the South Slavic Philologist. These magazines are published by the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. I'm a member of the seven scientific committees of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts and I'm also the deputy secretary of the department for literature and arts in the Academy of Science and Arts of Republika Srpska. I'm a member of the editorial board of the Encyclopedia Republika Srpska. As you can see, I have a lot of duties, a lot of things on my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, I do see it, and thank you for that, and that's why I just wanted to highlight it's in fact in your CV, which is within your report. Also, you identify in your report various publications that you've written; is that correct? And I think you list approximately four pages worth of publications in which you've authored or co-authored in specifically the science of linguistic and dialects, or the study of dialectology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I've published around 200 scientific and professional papers published by the Serbian Academy of Sciences and other publishers in the country and abroad. I am also a member of the commission for the general South Slavic Atlas with the International Committee of Slavic Experts, and I'm also on the editorial board for the General Carpathian Dialect Atlas. I have also published about 40 dialectological maps for Slavic languages in the Carpathian area. Most of my works concern dialectology, although I'm also concerned with the history of the Serbian literary language.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when were you first contacted by the Beara Defence team to review and analyse certain intercept conversations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: This happened in October last year. I got a telephone call. I believe you were in Sarajevo at the time, and that's when our cooperation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to October 2007, had you known any members, personally, of the Beara Defence team, including the lawyers or the support staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anybody before the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to October 2007, did you know Mr. Ljubisa Beara or any members of his family?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: People are familiar with the family name "Beara" because the most famous footballer's name was Beara. But I was not familiar with the name of Mr. Ljubisa Beara. In October, when you contacted me, I didn't know who you were talking about. It was only when I met with the lawyers in Belgrade that I actually learned the name of the gentleman in whose defence I was supposed to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record's clear, you didn't know any members of his family either; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anybody then. I subsequently met his wife, but the answer would be "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us briefly what task, if any, was assigned to you for purposes of analysing these purported intercept conversations? What was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: My assignment was -- at least that's how I understood it -- to look at the alleged intercepts, to analyse them, and to see whether they could be attributed to Mr. Beara, whether the text or the words that he allegedly uttered were in those intercepts, because in the transcripts that I had available to me for the most part alleged that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And were you given any other assignment over the course of our professional relationship since October 2007 to do any other sort of analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when I was told that I should also pay attention to the semantic -- to the meaning of some of the words, to look at that as well. I believe that the word in question is the word "triage" and also to look at the name "Ljubo" and the status of the name "Ljubo" in among the Serbian names. My task was to see who the name "Ljubo" could be referring to based on the literature and on my experience. These were the two things that I was supposed to pay particular importance to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Professor, we're going to turn to a couple things, and you're going to help us have a better understanding of your report. And preliminarily I'm going to ask you some general questions, and if you would be kind enough to explain to me what these terms mean. For example, the first term, so that we're on the same page, can you tell me what is the study of linguistics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "the study of linguistics"? In what terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The study of languages, in general, and then we're going to go specifically to dialects. So dialectology and linguistics, can you explain to us what that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The dialectology, you mean? Dialectology is a linguistic scientific discipline that deals with the dialects of different people. Dialectology, as a discipline in Europe, took off the ground and gained credibility in the 19th century. In our parts, it was in the beginning of the 20th century when dialectology became known as a scientific discipline. In Serbia, the first dialectologist was Vuk Karadzic. He was the one who started the first division of dialects. Dialectology is very important as a discipline, which is corroborated by the fact that in Serbia, two major linguists of the 20th century were primarily dialectologists. They were Aleksandar Belic [phoen], who was the founder of dialectology as a scientific discipline, who was a member of all the Slavic academies of science. And his best disciple, Mr. Pavel Ilic, was a member of eight academies of science among which the American Academy of Science, the Russian Academy of Science, the Academy of Science of Vienna and Serbia. He was also the dialectologist for the Encyclopedia Britannica. He authored the entry on dialects. Dialectology occupies a very high position as a science, and this arises from the matter that it deals with. Dialects are an inexhaustible treasure trove of data and information about the life of a people, of a nation. When it comes to linguistic facts that are available to a people, this reflects its entire history, its entire past, relationship in society, culture, ethnology, the spiritual and material culture as well. Dialects provide information which are of great value, of great value for several disciplines, for interdisciplinary research, and that is why dialectology is such a reputable science, and that's why it holds such a reputable position in linguistics. For example, the science of names or onomasticon, comprising the names of people, rivers and mountains, reflect the traces of all the civilizations that have lived in an area. We know perfectly well today that even long before Cleopatra's romances with Roman emperors, most of our rivers were called the Sava, the Drava, the Danube, the Morava, and others. These facts speak of the importance of dialectology as a scientific discipline. And like among the Serbs, among the Croats, the leading linguists of the past century and today are primarily dialectologists; for example, Brozovic, who is the leading Croatian linguistic, is primarily a dialectologist. And there is one more thing I would like to add, if I may. Dialects are threatened, they are at risk. Dialectology is hard pressed for time because civilization, with all its different forms of literacy, is suppressing dialects. It threatens them with complete extermination, and that is why dialectologists are hard pressed to complete the task that they haven't completed, and we in the Balkans are lagging behind in many things, dialectology not being an exception. Moreover, I would like to say that our dialects, the Serbian and Croatian dialects, and Bosniak as well, needless to say, are very interesting from the point of view of topology. They show that the history of the area has given us such a variety -- such a mosaic of dialects, such relationships which are very often a rarity in European terms. Our accent, our polithemy [phoen], our dialects, are a rarity, a very specific feature in planetary terms. Many foreigners have tried successfully to write books about our dialects, because our dialects are a challenge, they are inspirational, even for foreign scientists who have often dealt with the issue of our dialects.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And I'm not a linguist or a dialectologist, but I would like to clarify a couple of things. You mentioned that dialects provide us with a treasure trove of information on the life of a people and a nation. But what I would like to know specifically from you, Professor, is: Can you obtain information about an individual person from his dialect and the characteristics that he may use in his speech or pattern of speech? Is that something that's within this field?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify two things. One thing would be the research of dialects on the ground, when you actually investigate the autochthonous people who are often illiterate and who use a certain dialect. This is where a dialect can easily be observed, very clearly be observed. Truth be told, there are no pure dialects anywhere, because civilization has had its impact on all the dialects. We may be talking about that a little bit later. And when it comes to the educated people who are not part of the rural population, who are not the autonomous -- the allochthonous inhabitants of rural areas, then the task becomes a bit more difficult. But there is an old truth which says that some things cannot be hidden. One of them is cough, the other is love, the third is poverty, and the fourth one is dialect or speech. These cannot be covered up or hidden. The difference between the research of orthodox dialects and the attempts to determine, in a literate or educated man, his affiliation, the difference is the following: In a dialect, you can find the traces of literary speech, and in an educated person you are looking for traces of a dialect. In other words, the proportions are reverse or they oppose each other. We're talking about reverse proportions. In any case, it's very difficult or almost impossible to hide one's dialectological origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So am I correct if I say that dialectal characteristics can be used as reliable personal identifiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The degree of reliability in determining the identity is directly proportional to the quantity of linguistic facts and the core of facts available to the expert who wishes to determine the identity in question. The more -- the wealthier the core of linguistic facts, the higher the chances of success. Viscosity of linguistic fact core makes the task more difficult. Out in the field, when a dialect is being researched, the situation is much more favourable for the researcher. The researcher has questionnaires, masters the subject matter at hand, solicits discourse from the interlocutor, forms terms which are relevant to the researcher to reach a conclusion. In cases like this, you have what you have. You have to work with what you've been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll get back to the linguistic corpus as you identify it in your report, but what I'm asking you is whether or not we can use dialectal characteristics as personal identifiers. Can you tell, from listening or reading someone's text, whether or not they came from a certain region or from another region, or from hearing their voice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Mainly, it can be determined. From personal experience, I can tell you that I grew up in Bosnia, for instance. The dialect there is Herzegovinian Krajina. This is a new Stokavian dialect. For a long time, I spoke Ijekavian dialect in Novi Sad and Belgrade, and as the director of Serbia language of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, I spoke Ijekavian, but then I switched to Ekavian, which is not difficult. But I never, in speaking with people I knew or did not know, I never wanted to hide my identity. They used to ask me, for hundreds of times, whether I originated from Uzice. It is a town in Western Serbia. The dialect spoken there -- the base dialect is the same as in my case, the Ijekavian. And before departing to The Hague, when I spoke to Madam Beara, when we met, she said I spoke -- I was speaking like somebody from Uzice, that I lengthened some vowels like the people in Uzice. When we talk about dialectological characteristics to determine somebody's origin, we have to deal with the dialect as a whole, as a linguistic system, and in this very prominent role is played by somebody's accent, by somebody's prisodics [phoen]. This cannot be hidden. Serbian language contains four inventories of accents or stresses. Some two, some three, some have stresses like in Germany -- German or English. Then quantities after the accented syllable cannot be hidden, either. Practice has shown that people who do not have a long vowel after the stressed syllable cannot mimic that. I've listened to Belic's speech, a recording of his speech, and this Belic was the greatest linguist in Serbia, he originated from Belgrade, and he did not have the long vowels after the stressed syllables, which is characteristic of Belgrade. We also know people who are autochthonous Ekavians, and we know of people who best preserve the politomy [phoen]. The best Ekavian literally-linked language has been demonstrated by Professor Jovan Vukovic, who hailed from Dermitol [phoen] and lived in Sarajevo. Some people shove their vowels. There are different ways of expressing the same word. Some swallow their vowels. As Zivanovic used to write, somebody reduce their vowels. Some have "ch" and "dj" and not "ch" and "dj" as sounds. Some characteristics cannot be hidden. So as I said, speech tells volumes about an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and we'll get into that in more specific terms when we look at some of the intercepts before you, but we're talking about linguistics and linguistical characteristics, and what's a dialectal variant, if you can explain that to us? Just briefly, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Well, "dialectological variants," do you mean by that variants of this Serbian-Croatian literary language? It is known that recently, during the recent events in the Balkans, that the Croatian and Serbian linguistic community broke up, together with the common state, and it is known that Serbs and the Croats for 100 years used to have a common literary language, the Serbo-Croatian or Croat-Serbian. It was reached in the following manner: In Zagreb, after a lengthy discussion, very fierce debate in 1889, the Croatian Parliament, the Sabor, adopted the decision to promulgate the new Stokavian common Vuk Karadzic type of language as the official language. Immediately after that in Zagreb, they published the instruments -- the textbooks of that language. 1892, Ivan Broz published the Croatian orthography. Then Tomo Maratic [phoen], a major scientist, published the grammar and stylistics of the Croatian or Serbian language. And then in 1902, Ivan Broz and his uncle, Vrankovic [phoen], published the dictionary of the Croatian language. In the preambles and the forewords of all these publications, it is written that they were modelled after Vuk Karadzic and his most prominent follower, Ljubo Danicic and that they used examples for their textbooks from Vuk Karadzic and Danicic's works. Maratic explained this by saying that he did so in his desire to take from the best, and Vuk was, in his words, the best among us, what Cicero was for the Romans, Vuk Karadzic was for us. These were the times when people wanted to strive for some common purposes, and therefore we received a common language. It was never the same, because there were, from the very beginning, some regional variance and differences. History made sure that the eastern variant of the language remains Ekavian and that Zagreb spoke Ijekavian. There were attempts to unify those, but they failed. There were consistent differences between the eastern and the western variant in the lexic, in words, and this is why in Zagreb, just as other Slavic languages under the Hapsburg monarchy, translated Germanic words, in the fear of Germanisation, into their languages, whereas in Serbia we adopted words. In Serbia, for instance, it was schnitzel. In Zagreb it was "odrezak." So there were linguistic norms, prescribed norms, but of course in life the linguistic practice differed from the norm. What is the most important for our story in all this is when it comes to the "jat," the long "jat," that's the Ijekavian reflex of the "jat," it is -- so that this "jat" is reflected in "dijeta" [phoen] and "lijepo" [phoen], as prescribed by orthography, but in speech from Zagreb, you can hear "lijepo" or "dijeta," very short "jat." This illustrates the dialectal -- dialectological variance, and this gave birth to divergent languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now, I think we understand dialectal variance a little bit. And I'm getting this from -- just so -- if you can follow along --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I did not hear it. Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Professor. I'd like to direct your attention briefly to the last page of your report, which is page 30, and that's why I'm asking you about the dialectal variance and the linguistical characters. And just so I can get a brief answer on this. And we'll get back to the different accents and the dialects and the regions from which they come. But my question, if you look on the last page of your report, the second-to-last paragraph, you reference morphological feature, and what I'd just like to know, you reference a word called morphological feature and what I'd like to just know, even briefer than your last answer, if you can provide us with a better explanation or understanding of what a morphological feature is. And I could direct your attention, if the Court doesn't mind, it's the second-to-last paragraph, in the middle of that sentence -- or in the middle of the paragraph, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: In the middle? I'm not sure whether we have the same texts. Do you mean the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The second-to-the-last paragraph, so I think it's page 29 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to this. I just want to have a foundation and a basis so that we can have a discussion here and have a better understanding. The paragraph starts, Professor, as follows -- are you on the last page? You can put your headset directly on top of your head. That might help you a little.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I'm too short. I'll have to go upwards in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Can you start speaking so I can check whether I can hear you? Now it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The paragraph -- second-to-the-last paragraph of your report of the 18th of April, 2008, starts as follows: "A comparison of the language of the alleged intercepts and Mr. Beara's current manner of speech has brought to the surface the diametric opposition." You go on to identify these dialectal variants and this morphological feature. And if you look specifically on page 29 -- so turn to your report, which is in B/C/S, on page 29.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you see the highlighted word on the very last sentence on page 29 of the B/C/S, which says "sjor"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's that line immediately above that, and you use the word "morphological feature" and all I'm trying to do so that I can better understand your report, Professor, is to have you explain what that means. And we'll come back to the conclusion. So just tell me from a linguistical standpoint or a dialectologist's standpoint, what does it mean when you reference a morphological feature? What are morphological features?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Morphological features are forms -- is a conjugation and a declination, forms of cases of nouns, pronouns, adjectives and numbers, and conjugation refers to verbs. Then we have phonemes, which are sounds, and these are forms, these are words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just tell me, if you can just as briefly, what a lexical domain is? And, again, you reference that in your report, I think, three words after "morphological feature," so just so we could have a better understanding of that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: "Lexical domain" means words. Language, as a system, has several domains; phonological, morphological, lexic and syntactical. Lexic is the most open domain to foreign influences. There is a proverb, there are no limitations, there are no boundaries to a language with words which are borrowed from other languages. They follow technology that we borrow from other civilization as well. For instance, words referring to the material, spiritual culture, these are the vocabulary that we adopt, this is the lexic. And this domain contains most borrowed words and terms in any language, because this subsystem is the most open of them all. Our dialect reflects the very tumultuous history of this area. There were guests arriving here, both invited and uninvited. In the literal -- or along the coastline, you have many Romanisms. In the north, Vojvodina, we have many borrowed words from the Hungarian. Then all over the place, we had many Turkish borrowed terms because of five centuries of Ottoman domination, then from German language. Then when ideologies converged, we have many Russian words as borrowed words, and now we cannot defend ourselves from Anglocisms. This has always been so and it will always be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a word that you mentioned earlier today. When you discuss these regions and the influences by other entities within the region of the former Yugoslavia, you mentioned on page 10, line 3, the word "topology." Could you just define that for us? I think we understand what you mean. It's not in your report. It was actually page 10, line 3 of today's transcript, Professor. So just tell me what you mean when you say the word "topology."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Typology, like as in type, typology. This is a typo here. Typology of dialects, types, classes, categories, classification of dialects, this is typology. This is not topology. It must have been a mistake by either me or whoever transcribed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We just wanted to clarify that. A couple more definitions and I'm sorry for that, but I just want to make sure that I have a better understanding of your report. What is a linguistic diachronic or diachronics within linguistics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: This is a study of a language through a historical period, diachronical study. Diachronic linguistics or dynamic linguistics means that it studies a history of a form or of a language. Synchrony is opposite of diachrony. Synchrony means right now this is a study of languages or a linguistic system or a certain feature in a cross-section in time, a snapshot in time. This today means this description of today's status of the linguistic system of a language. Diachrony is history and synchrony is today. This is in the most simplest terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just tell us the various regions, republics of former Yugoslavia, did it have a variant from one republic to the other as to what the dialect was that was spoken by the people residing in a certain area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croatian linguistic area is divided into three dialectic complexes, the Stokavian, the Kajkavian, and the Stokavian -- and the Cakavian. Stokavian is the most widely spread, originated in the medieval Serbian states and adjoining areas. The Cakavian dialect was created in the medieval Dalmatian Croatia and the adjoining areas, and the Kajkavian dialect originated from the Pannonian area of today's Croatia, of Slavonija. Boundaries of these three dialects moved. There were migrations which are a very important fact of the dialectology, both Serbian and Croatian. With the invasion of the Ottoman Turks, there were mass migrations, the Cakavian dialect boundary was moved and Cakavian dialect expanded at the expense of the Cakavian due to those migrations. Cakavian dialect's boundary used to be more to the west than genetically Stokavian and Cakavian are closer together, whereas Kajkavian dialect is closer to Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, but the transcript is having a little bit of trouble keeping up with us, and I apologise for that. And just so that I'm clear, you mentioned -- I'm probably going to butcher it, Stokavian and then you also mentioned Kajkavian, and the one that we didn't get was the Cakavian, which is "C," with an accent on it, a-k-a-v-i-a-n; correct? It just didn't come up on the transcript, and I want to verify that that's the third one. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Well, for our purposes, the Cakavian dialect is very important. Kajkavian is of no import for us today dealing with this matter. The Cakavian originated and was created in the medieval Dalmatian Croatia, in the hinterland, very narrow swath of hinterland, and on the islands. The Unacetina [phoen] line was the western boundary of the Cakavian which was pushed back due to migrations. Is there a need to further analyse the distinction between the Cakavian and the Stokavian, or would this suffice for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the time being, it does suffice. Thank you. I just wanted to make sure all three were properly in the record so that we can follow it together. Now, within each of these, are there various or variant dialects? For example, in the Cakavian one, are there different dialects that are from that region, which is the Dalmatian, as you described, and Croatian region?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, the dialectal core of Serbian, Croatian and Bosniak, very differentiated. There is a jigsaw puzzle of those dialects, and within the dialects, of course, there are differences. Within the Cakavian dialect, there are three different modes of speech. We have the Ekavian and Cakavian in the west, like deta [phoen]. Further to the south, we have Ikavian, like in dica [phoen], which is spoken in Split, which is very important for us for this case, the Ikavian. And there is an Ekavian-Ikavian transitional dialect which is not of interest to us. And in the very south, the island of Lastovo speaks Ijekovski, Ijekavian, and there are differences between Stokavians, Ikavians, Ekavians and Ijekavians. Cakavians do not have Ikavski and Ijekovski. We are going to discuss this further on. In the distribution and classification of dialects, the sound "jat" is the most important element to distinguish the dialects among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we will -- trust me, we will get back to this "jat" and to discuss that among other features and variants within the language, but right now I'd like for the Court, with its permission, to direct their attention and my learned friends to appendix 3 of your report, which is a dialect map. And I happen to have the original book that I think you referenced. With the Court's permission, I have provided my learned friends the book so they could see it. This is the only original we have. I think it's better colour-coded, so if the Court doesn't mind, although it's in e-court, maybe we could just very briefly go through the different regions within this book. And it's three pages, two of which are attached to his report, so it would be this page and this page, and then also ... thank you. And, Professor, as we're putting the book on the ELMO, can you tell me, what is this book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the Encyclopedia of Yugoslavia. The entry is Serbo-Croatian, Croat Serbian language, Croatian or Serbian language, and here you can see a summary of the history of the national language, the history of the literary language, and the dialectological complex of the Serbs and the Croats. The book came from the hands of the two leading Serbian and Croatian linguists of their time. Those were Pavle Ilic, a member of the academy that I've already mentioned and another member of the academy, Dalibor Brozovic, the leading Croatian and Serbian linguists, and the latter is still alive today. This is a summary of what can be found in the Encyclopedia of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And because you use it, sir, in your appendix 3, I just wanted the Court and my learned friends to have it so they could look at it as well, and it's a little better because we didn't have colour copies to attach to your report. The first one you can see, which is on the screen hopefully before you and directly to the right on the ELMO is the Cakavian one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here, yes, yes, this is the Cakavian dialect, of course. Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, it says so right on top, right on the top of the page. And below that, although we can't see it on the ELMO yet, is the different dialects from that specific region, and if the Court permits, if the usher could just zoom out a little. You can see it there, and I think the grid below on the lower left-hand side -- if we could have the whole page, that would be helpful, if possible. On the lower left-hand side of that page, it actually highlights with different colours what the various dialects are that you previously identified for us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could turn to the next page, which is a two-page map of the former Yugoslavia and various regions, which identify the Stokavian; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then the third one, which you say is not necessarily relevant to --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- our purposes is the third page, the very next page, which is the Kajkavian?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Kajkavian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as to each --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: It's irrelevant for today's story, that's for sure. And as for the Cakavian, only the Ikavian-Cakavian is interesting. That's the speech commonly used in Split and its environs. That's what we are interested in today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I just wanted us to have it for purposes of completeness so that we could see the entire former region and how the various dialects were distributed or utilized in the former Yugoslavia. So with the Court's permission and the usher's assistance, if we can please turn to the first photograph, which is the Cakavian, yes, that one, with the various dialects on the bottom that we see, correct, and I think you were proceeding to tell us that it's this one that for our purposes is important. So can you please set forth for us the differences, if any, in the dialects within these regions where they spoke Cakavian?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The differences exist within Cakavian, but they're of not so much importance for us. In the west, there is the Ekavian variant, which can be found in the basis of the words such as in "pesma," and it is also preserved in the declination. For example, we say "ugradu" [phoen], and in the old dialect they used to say "vagrada" [phoen], and this has been preserved. And now in the Ekavian, which is in blue, we have also a transitional area Ekavian Ikavian, where according to the Myer and Kabinsky [phoen] rules, the "jat" results in the vowel E or I, and in the south we have the island of Lastovo where people use Ijekavian variant of the dialect. I don't know how interesting this might be for you when it comes to the phonetics that analyse or differentiate the Cakavian dialect. We can also speak about the semivowel, the short, accentuated semivowel. For example, on the island of Krk we have a long vowel that results in an "a" and the shortened "o," whereas on the island of Cres, the long and the short vowel result in different vowels, and also when it comes to the Cakavian features, we have an entire Cakavian area that is swamped under the Roman influences. This is what we call the so-called Adriatisms or the adopted words. First they were called Adriatisms, and now they are called Dalmatianism upon Brozovic's proposal, and that is what is used today in the linguistic science. These are various features that have developed under the influence of the Romanic neighbours with whom these people had to coexist, and this is what we can find in "L," such in Ljubo, which transformed in a "J", Ljubo, and then we have the transformation of "M" into "N," and hence the anecdotes involving the words "I am" or "I am not," "yes" and [indiscernible] that we heard from Mr. Beara. What we're interested in here is the Ikavian Cakavian dialect as spoken in Split, and what I'm saying is that this is the only type of Cakavian that we are interested in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that, and we'll come back and focus particularly on that. My general question to you, Professor -- and thank you, Mr. President and Madam Usher. I think we don't need the book any further, but I'd like if we just make sure the colours are properly photocopied. If not, I would just ask that we will amend it to put the three pages so that the Court has the proper colouring of the various dialects within the region. But we can discuss that at another time, if the Court wishes. If I may proceed. So, Professor, my question to you is -- yes, thank you. Are these dialects actually distinct and unique, and can a person such as yourself, a linguist and a dialectologist, can you, immediately upon hearing one's speech, identify primarily from what region a person may come from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Dialects differ. They bear different names because of the differences. Their different names reflect their differences. That's one thing. Second of all, when it comes to identifying somebody, there are two approaches present or two angles. The first principle is the principle of elimination. I have to eliminate where the person is not from, if you know that person. Dialects, when we talk about people speaking Stokavian and Cakavian, they have different variants, and the differences are even bigger. There are differences within dialects within groups of people speaking the same dialect. These differences are not always of the same intensity or of the same type, but they are clearly discernible. An expert, a competent expert, that is, can, without any major problems, identify the person as speaking a certain dialect if that person is using the dialect. If you give a -- provide a dialectologist with five tapes with five different dialects, he will listen to them, and within ten minutes he will be able to identify the speech that the dialects come from. This is for sure. And, finally, ultimately, even people who are not experts, who are not competent, who are not specialists in the field, based on the experience from their contacts with people from different areas, people can actually tell. Also, they can do it based on the names. For example, if people speak like me, based on the name, they can be originated back to the Western Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I know we eliminated one of them, the Kajkavian one. Can you draw a distinction ever so briefly between the Stok avian and the Kajkavian speech patterns and the relevance to your task that was assigned? And just if you can, show us or draw the distinction between the two, if possible.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you're referring to Cakavian and not Kajkavian. We have eliminated the Kajkavian. Are you referring to the area from which Mr. Beara hails and where he comes from, where he resided? If the answer is "yes," then it's Cakavian, not Kajkavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken, but I thought I had it right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have misspoken, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between Stokavian and Cakavian, can you draw any distinction so that we could better understand it between the two and what relevance it had to your assignment, if any?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The basic and the most discernible difference between the three speeches that have given these speeches, their names is the form of the pronoun in German "vas" [phoen], or in Latin -- if that would be "quid," that would be "stokaj" [phoen] and "cha" [phoen]. That's the pronoun that has been given the names to these speeches. The next difference is between the Stokavians and the Cakavians comes from the accents, from the prosody. The Stokavians have two short accents, the short rising, as in "djena" [phoen] and "zesta" [phoen], and they have a descending accent in the vocative, as in "djena" and "zestro" [phoen]. This is very unique in European terms. Furthermore, the difference between Stokavians and Cakavians also arises from the different vowels they use. Stokavian people speaking Stokavian have explosing [as interpreted] affects, at least one. They have a "dje" and a "gdje" and many have even a "dze." For example, "major," in Cakavian it is "meja." We have "dje" and they don't have it, and many of our speeches also have a "dze." Obviously, this is in dialects. In Stokavian, the noun may be expanded into "craljevi" [phoen] and "crajevi" [phoen], and in Cakavian it is "kralaj" [phoen] and "kraj" [phoen]. The vowels and the consonants are under the influence of the Roman speech or the Roman dialect. There is a lot more Roman words, and in our parts there are a lot more Turkish words, German words, and those influences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for those examples. I know there are many, many, many more, but let's just, for the purpose of brevity, just try to give these couple of examples and we'll go on with the rest of your report where you can highlight for us, if you don't mind, Professor, some of these other distinguishing features and variants. What I'd like to know, sir, here is you mentioned that you reviewed four things in connection with the intercepts on Mr. Beara, the NIOD report, statements from witnesses, the transcript and a short biography. Can you share with us who provided you with the background of Mr. Beara's biography?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: As for the background of Mr. Beara's biography, it was one of the lawyers who has provided me with those. One of you gave that to me, either John Ostojic or Stanisic, or somebody in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the person in Belgrade with whom I think you met when I was there on a couple of occasions was one of our investigators, Mr. Milan Stanic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Milan Stanic, yes, yes, that's what I said, Mr. Stanic. Milan Stanic was the one, I suppose. I suppose that Milan Stanic gave this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter who gave it to you. Just share with us what is the information that was provided to you regarding Mr. Beara's biography, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beara's biography is something that was necessary. I needed it. I was supposed to elaborate my methodology based on that biography. I was supposed to elaborate my methodology based on that biography. I was supposed to adopt an approach based on that biography. I wanted to see where he resided, where he worked, and I needed to compare the dialectology situations or the speech variants in the various places where he resided, where he grew up, and to compare that with the language of those alleged intercepts. Since he grew up in Sarajevo, and when he turned 19 he moved to the coast, then he spent most of his career in the Cakavian territory, and he often travelled across the hinterland inhabited by the Herzegovina and Krajina dialect-speaking people. In the transcripts I was looking for the links that might tie the transcripts with Sarajevo or the area where he subsequently lived and worked. I must admit that I had expected to find some traces of the dialects from his youth and childhood. Let's be clear on one thing. When you analyse a speech or the linguistic patterns used by a high-ranking officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, then you have to start from the fact that that person will probably speak a very correct literal language and that the dialect or the localisms are a minority. They may creep in as something that cannot be hidden and that will reveal the origin of that person. I was also interested in the fact whether the literal language spoken by that person, whether it was the so-called western variant or the eastern variant, as spoken in the former common state, and this is where I wanted to find my departure point or the orientation point from which I could see how things stood. Obviously, most of the work I carried out and most of the effort I invested before I actually met with Mr. Beara and before my conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you give -- did you request that you meet with Mr. Beara so that you could fully understand his linguistics characteristics and the dialect that he may be speaking today? Did you meet with him, actually?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I must say that if I'm not mistaken, quite a long time ago I expressed my wish to meet with Mr. Beara. It took a while for my wish to be granted, and we actually met on the 7th and 8th of April this year in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just briefly before our next break, if you can tell us who was present during the first meeting you had with Mr. Beara at the UNDU?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Mr. John Ostojic, Ms. Jelena Dzambasovic, the interpreter, and the lawyer from -- he was tall and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can I help you? Chris Meek?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Chris Meek, yes, yes, yes. He was there the first day, and the following day it was just Mr. Ostojic, Ms. Dzambasovic and myself on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell us with respect to the -- what was your purpose for wanting to meet with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of my cooperation with the Defence counsel, I was faced with a major handicap, which was the lack of any audio recordings. I only had the transcripts of the alleged intercepted conversations, very poor in linguistical terms, and we will speak about the difficulties that I encountered there a bit later, and I wanted to hear the way Mr. Beara speaks now. I wanted to meet him and see how the written language, as encountered in the transcripts that are attributed to Mr. Beara compare with his actual speech today. I wanted to draw a comparison and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, in essence, you were doing an evaluation and analysis of his current speech pattern, despite the fact that it was 13 years after the purported intercept conversations that were captured, from 1995 to 2008?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit that I was very surprised with what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, we'll --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: -- in my conversation with Mr. Beara. As it turned out, in free communication with the Defence lawyer, the interpreter, and me as the expert, he used the Cakavian dialect as spoken in Split. This is the typical Cakavian Split dialect. Now, when he uses the features of a literary language, then as a rule it is the Croatian variant of the once common language which is today known as the Croatian language. I was more than surprised with the fact that after such a long time, he still uses the Split dialect, and my general observation, which will be elaborated a bit further, is that his current speech is in sharp collision with what can be found in the transcripts of the alleged intercepts. There is a very sharp collision between those transcripts and the speech pattern that he uses today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me just spend a couple of minutes that we have with respect to those meetings. The first meeting, you did basically observations between the conversations that Mr. Beara and others in the room had, and you were basically observing us talking and discussing various things; would that be accurate? And I apologise for leading. I just want to get through this little section. Is that right, Professor Remetic, that the first day, you were observing as I was talking with Mr. Beara, and on the second day, just to show somewhat of a difference, you were actually asking him certain questions and certain words, and you were taking notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I remember the first sentence that Mr. Beara uttered. He asked Ms. Dzambasovic, "Why are you so pale?" That was the first thing he said. I must say that I was surprised. The time that I spent in Scheveningen and the conversation that I had with Mr. Beara was a major experience for me and a major revelation which was rife with surprises. In that case, I could do what I am not allowed to do as a dialectologist. When a dialectologist goes into the field to talk to people, there are no suggestions allowed or any questions. This is strictly forbidden. On the first day, I had a notebook in my hand and I was eavesdropping on the conversation between the people. It was a rather relaxed conversation. The mood was relaxed. He was talking to -- Beara was talking to his lawyer, the interpreter. There was a cup of coffee in front of everybody. They were joking. I was listening to them and I was taking notes. I was there in my capacity as a dialectologist, and I was very surprised when I heard him speak, the way he spoke. And when I realised that I was dealing with a person of a very high level of intelligence, very cooperative, very noble in his willingness to cooperate, I could even put some questions to him, I could ask him about certain linguistic forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to clear up these two things. And just so the record's clear, you kept and created notes during those two meetings which we have for the record and as my learned friend knows, we've identified them or a copy of those notes as 2D584; is that correct, Professor Remetic? Not that you need to know the number, but you had provided us an original and we had copied the notes from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I have provided you my original notes. I didn't know that you would ask for them. I was doodling, I was drafting my report. I underlined some things in black or green, I crossed some things over. This was my working material, as you could see, and I've provided you with that material and I've kept a copy for myself, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we've sent it forward to the Prosecution, and I think I got it -- when did you provide that to us; a couple of weeks ago when I saw you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to come back to an issue that you said the first sentence or the first words you heard Mr. Beara utter was with respect of Ms. Dzambasovic's pale complexion. Now, can you tell us, in the different dialects, how would you say the word "pale"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what it's all about. Obviously, we're dealing with the "jat." In Ekavian, it would be "bleda," in Ikavian it would be "bljeda," in Ijekavian it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You're going a little way too fast, and we're having a hard time hearing even the distinction between the three. So if you can just please kindly -- and I know we're ready for a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And maybe we could take a deep breath and take a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I was going to suggest. Twenty-five minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Professor Remetic. If we could proceed, but if I could just clarify the last -- before the break, we just had a little discussion of the word "pale," and I'm going to spell it, and I ask my colleague if I can lead a little bit on this so we have it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding, sir, that there's at least three ways that you could say the word "pale" in Serbian, depending on the dialect. The first one would be "bleda," which is b-l-e-d-a, the second one is "blijeda," which is b-l-i-j-e-d-a, and the third one is "bljeda," which is b-l-j-e-d-a. Am I correct that those are the three that you were trying to convey to us before the break?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the three basic ways. Of course, "bleda" is literally prescribed, "blijeda" is also literally, and "bljeda" with l-j is a dialect form of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the third one. Can you tell us of those three, which one Mr. Beara utilised in describing Ms. Dzambasovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Before me, I have my notes, and the first word is "blijeda," and the next is "bleda." When I first heard that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. If you could be kind enough, and I think we have it, but just for our purposes here, to spell it out as well. And you have the transcript in front of you, and I know your English is limited, but I think you can see when they don't pick up some of the words that you're using. So, again, the first word that you used is "blijeda," B-L-I-J-E-D-A; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first one is "blijeda," which is the norm of the Serbian and Croatian literary language. In the Serbs of the Ijekavian type and in the Croatian language of the literary type. "Bleda," B-L-E-D-A, is the norm of the Serbian literary language, the Ekavian variant; for instance, as spoken in Belgrade. And "blida," B-L-I-D-A, is a dialect. This is not a literary norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were you able to derive anything from the characteristics of Mr. Beara's speech in utilising these first words in your first impression?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: As I said, the "jat" sound, how it is reflected in the dialects, is the most important element in classifying the Croatian and Serbian and Bosniak dialects, and from the very moment I heard "ubljdila," "going pale," U-B-L-J-D-I-L-A, and "stosimi bljeda," "why are you so pale," B-L-J-E-D, that what I had confronted was a Croatian literary language. And the Croatian spoken variant of the literary language, because in Croatian textbooks it is prescribed that it should stand as B-L-I-J-E-D-A, but in spoken practice mainly, this is reduced to a single syllable pronunciation of "blijeda," B-L-I-J-E-D-A. "Blijeda" can be heard in Serbian speeches, speech types -- yes, this is correct, yes -- can be heard, as I said, in Serbian speech types of the Adriatic hinterland, where Mr. Beara often resided as part of his duties. This is the way it is spoken in Zagorje, or the hinterland, in Dalmatia, where Serbs live, in Lika, and it was clear to me from the very first moment that there were no traces of the Sarajevo speech type where -- which would be "blijeda" or I-J-E-D-A. So he did not speak, in terms of dialect or literary language, like the inhabitants of his native Sarajevo. I had a dilemma, whether the word "bljed," B-L-J-E-D originated from the Croatian spoke literary language as spoken in Split. When one tries to speak correctly, using the literary language, or whether it went for the reflex or influence of Serbian speech types of the hinterland of the coast, as I mentioned. Very soon, I got my answer, and on the first page of my notes, which look like this [indicates] because I did not know in advance that this would be used subsequently - this is my working material - very soon I heard Ikavian features instead of Sarajevoian Uvijek, always, U-V-I-J-E-K, and what is also the literary form. Mr. Beara would always say "uvik," U-V-I-K. Furthermore, similar examples were to follow. For instance, "Dida," instead of "Djed," D-J-E-D or "Djed," among the Serbs, Ekavians, or "deda" like in Ekavian, then the verb "triba," T-R-I-B-A, after ten or so minutes, to my surprise, I realised and I was surprised, but I realised that Mr. Beara, in free, open conversation with his interlocutors and people he knew, and in that context I was there for the first time, that he speaks the Cakavian-Ikavian Split dialect or speech type. And it will later transpire, when he would be speaking literary forms, that he would be using, as a rule, the Croatian or western variant of the once-common language, which is today the Croatian literary language. Mr. Beara's speech on the 7th and the 8th, and the language of the transcripts are -- as a rule, are two different, disparate categories. They're incompatible, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll come back to that specific opinion that you have a little later, as it's reflected in your report. I'd like to ask you now, and we're going to move along in your report, if possible, but first: Did you feel that the seven to eight hours was adequate and sufficient for you to evaluate the speech pattern of Mr. Beara in order to assist you in formulating your analysis and opinions that you're providing in your report and here today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The seven or eight hours spent with Mr. Beara, which were filled not only by his speech, understandably we spoke also, Defence counsel spoke, I joined in the conversation, I asked him questions, understandably is not sufficient to write a dissertation or a study about his speech patterns. One would need a larger corpus of discourse. Let me remind you that my doctoral thesis was written on the basis of 200 hours of recordings. This is something completely different. But this, however, was sufficient to draw conclusions to get the general picture, and Mr. Beara identified himself in terms of his today's speech patterns during the first or initial stage of my conversation. And on the first page of my notes, I jotted down the most material bit, and it is sufficient, when it comes to the content of the transcripts, which hopefully we'll elaborate on later, is later scarce, very poor, very limited. In terms of subject matter, it's very narrow, and in terms of quantity, it is insufficient. But most probably we will cover these later on. So it was sufficient to hear Mr. Beara, that 17 years after he left Split, that he is in good command of the Split Cakavian speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your professional experience, Mr. Remetic, can a person shift from one dialect to another within a relative brief period, given that you observed and conducted examination of Mr. Beara both in a casual as well as a formal question-and-answer session? Can a person shift that quickly or are you, as a professional, able to detect specifically those dialects and those differences in his dialect and speech?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: When it comes to Mr. Beara, he did not switch that quickly. As I know he spent some 20 years living in that area, I must say that I gave it quite a bit of thought and I mused how he pulled it off that, in front of me, to deviate from his dialect and to accept -- to suppress his own dialect, to adopt a different dialect, and to stick to it after so many years. For me, this presented a great problem, to decipher this conundrum, if we depart from the presumption that the transcripts may be connected with the name of Mr. Beara. He was an Ikavian speaker before the end of the war. How could he have abandoned his speech patterns and then readopted, after the war, and during this middle period he spoke something else? For me, this is a challenge, I must tell you. And if you allow me and if this is the proper place to say it, I can tell you, as a person who is nearing his academic career, research career, a man with a wealth of experience, I've heard many dialects spoken out in the field, and had I -- if I were 30 years younger, I would have found a way to research, in depth, the speech patterns of Mr. Beara to see how could one switch to another dialect and to stick to it. This would be a very good subject matter for research, for study.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mention in your report various limitations or problems that you experienced in reviewing the documents that were provided to you, and directing your attention to Roman numeral VI of your report, Professor, you list specifically five. And just briefly, I'd like to go over them with you, although you've mentioned some of them, such as a lack of audio recording which would be beneficial and helpful to you. And the second aspect of it is you see the difficulty with the fragmentation of the linguistic expression of the alleged intercepts, and then you talk about number 3, which is the linguistic corpus, which I think in essence, and you correct me if I'm wrong -- which was the material that was provided to you was limited, in the sense in the number of conversations and/or the length of the conversation. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, all these things are true, and these presented difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you list two other limitations or problems that you experienced with respect to the material that was provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution, and that is I think you looked at some of the statements and you felt that there was choppiness or lack of clarity of the recording, based on specifically the handwritten transcripts. If you remember on some of them, they had specifically the three dots, which is standard for words that were omitted because they are unclear, ambiguous or indiscernible; that would be another problem that you saw within those manuscripts, if we can call them that; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you list out, as a fifth problem or limitation that you found particularly difficult was the orthographic and grammatical rules, and you identify enclitic and proclitic. And just for our benefit, could you expand on that and tell me what an enclitic and proclitic is, but very briefly, and why did you find that somewhat problematic for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Enclitics are words, in the Serbian language, which do not have their own independent stress but are pronounced together with the preceding words, and they such create a stress unit. And enclitics are usually truncated or shortened versions of verbs, pronouns, or ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In essence, really an enclitic is what goes at the end of a word and a proclitic is what goes at the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: At the end or after the words. The proclitics are words which do not have their own accent or stress, but form an accent unit with the ensuing word, the word they lean towards. There are rules of how enclitics and proclitics are to be written down, and there are -- there is the danger that less educated people may make mistakes in writing them down. For instance, the negation "nee," together with verbs, is to be written down separately, "nee" and then "radi," "nee jeda" [phoen], "doesn't eat," "nee prica" [phoen], "doesn't speak," but "neerad" [phoen], as a noun, has to be written as one word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think. I think that -- go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: And then from the erroneous transcription of proclitics and enclitics, I derived an opinion that the operators were not, if I dare say so, educated well enough, in terms of language, for that type of work. They had problems of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in that same section, you talk about orthographic -- orthography, as well as phonological principles, and is that basically what you were referencing now, those two concepts? Or if you like, you can explain those to us, and then we're going to move on to the specifics here as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Serbian, Croatian and Bosniak orthography, since everything derives from the Vuk Karadzic principles, is a phonological orthography, the so-called phonological orthography. This is the Vuk's rule: Write as you speak and read as written. Pursuant to those rules, there should be as many graphemes and phonemes, there should be as many letters as there are sounds, and everything should read as written. "Scheveningen" would be ten letters, ten sounds. "Sudnica" would be seven letters, seven sounds. There are exceptions, however, in orthography -- words or forms, rather, are written down in such a manner as it would be impossible to pronounce them, in concrete terms. "Ds" -- consonants "D" and "S," are different in terms of whether voiced or unvoiced in Serbian and Croatian and Bosniak language. When they co-locate, there is an automatic shift and an alternation. They are simulated by their characteristic of being voiced or unvoiced, and they cannot stand next to each other if they are different in this characteristic. In the nominative, "Sudac," in the genitive case, "Sudica," they cannot stand together, or "Vrabac" in the nominative case and "Vrabica." "D" and "S," "B" and "C" cannot be pronounced, but they are written down in this form because this is the correct orthography. And in certain transcripts, when they say "odseku," O-D-S-E-K-U, or "predsidnik" [phoen], from that I saw that they adhered to what they learnt in school. They did recall some of these things, because I'm sure that these things were not pronounced as they were transcribed. It is impossible to pronounce such clusters without much effort, and people on the battlefield have other things to occupy themselves with, and of course, this is not their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you this: You had the opportunity to review the witness statements or testimony of the various -- or some of the intercept operators. Were you able to use, as a baseline, or determine whether or not the operators used a certain technique or method in how they would capture the conversation, or would they just interpret the conversation as they wanted to, or what was their rule of thumb in capturing some of these conversations, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Objection. That's outside the field of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment while I have to deal with this. Do you wish to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can lay further foundation, if the Court wishes. I'll do that. I'll just ask him a question, and I think it will be clear to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Vanderpuye, because already as it is, it's getting very tiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, when we look at the fourth limitation that you have in your report under section 6, Roman numeral VI, you identify the sloppiness or choppiness of various intercept transcripts that you reviewed. Do you, sir, and have you had any experience with respect to listening to audio recordings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, "experience"? My own experience, do you mean, in my profession, or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in your profession.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: In my profession. In my experience, you mean. You know, I paid a lot of attention to the statements of these people, because we are colleagues in one way. I spent all my life recording in the field and listening to the recordings. I've even used the same technique. They mention Uher, and I used Uher to record thousands upon thousands of hours of conversations and dialects, and I even went to the Kladanj area, where some of the operators hail from. You will find it in my CV also. However, the circumstances under which I recorded were better or much better, my technique was always working properly and I never reused the same tapes. I would then listen to them in my house, in peace and quiet of my home, in ideal conditions, but there are always difficulties and there's always a lack of clarity when you're listening to these tapes, and I very often asked for the second opinion of my colleagues from the same profession, when I listened to things that I didn't find clear enough, and these people really worked under very difficult conditions. They had obsolete technique, and they had to re-use the same tapes, and they worked a lot. If you go on recording for four hours, it's very tiring, and it's a job that demands concentration, and especially when you listen to these tapes. It arises from statements that they would transcribe immediately after recording. They were already very tired, and I would say that their job was really very hard and their position was not enviable at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From reading the statements, did you rely on those statements from those various operators in formulating some of the opinions that you've reflected in your report of the 18th of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I don't remember having found a lot in the transcripts. What I noticed was that their language was very uniform. I did not notice anything in their language that would be uncommon for the dialect for that area. They are high school graduates. Only one was an engineer. Two had an associate degree. They come from an area that I'm very familiar with. I don't know whether the uniformity of the languages, the consequence of the fact that it was all typed by one and the same person. I wouldn't know that because I don't have any information about that. The only explanation I found for some interrupted conversation, when it says in the transcripts "unclear," "cannot be heard," I believe that you remember what I'm talking about, you will find it in transcripts, I found an explanation, people had problems with frequencies, they very often did not have a proper electricity source, they worked with batteries, and that would the explanation for the shortcomings in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if, within those statements that you reviewed, the intercept operators were instructed on how they should record the purported captured conversations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any instructions. I only remember, from their own words, that they were mostly Hamm operators, amateurs. There were no real professionals among them, as far as I can remember, but they had had some training courses at the very beginning, when the war started, and they had to pass a test, a theory and a test and a hands-on test.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Professor, if they used the phonological principles that you earlier described for us this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to belabour the point, but I think we're far afield of this witness's expertise as a forensic linguist or just as a linguist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is related, isn't it? I mean, I quite agree that it is not exactly bull's eye, but more or less it is related. Yes, go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Professor, I think? Do you want me to restate it for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you glean from the statements that you read of the intercept operators whether or not they used phonological principles similar to those which you've described earlier for us today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: They're not expected to use that, because they are not competent. When you record something as a dialectologist, then we record accents and all the nuances in the phonetics and the voices. But in their job, that was irrelevant. Nobody asked them to do that. They were not expected to do that. At least that's what I believe was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... opinions here.
