We're turning now, Professor, to the next section of your report, and if you'd like, you're welcome to follow along, which is Roman numeral VII of your report, where you talk about a general overview of Ljubisa Beara, Ljubisa Beara's language usage, and the factors influencing it. And you list three things that you mentioned earlier today, and I just want a clarification. You talk about, in this report, and you referenced a single-syllable reflexes of the long "jat," j-a-t. Then you go on to talk about the shorter infinitive, and then you talk about the future construction of the western type of lexical details. Those three independent -- I'd like to have you -- and I know you were anxious earlier to share with us specifically what the reflex of the long "jat" is, but now I think it might be a good time since we're going to try to go into the intercepts shortly. What is that "jat" j-a-t, as you reference it in the science of linguistics and the study of dialectology?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: "Jat" is the ancient Slavic vowel which was inherited by the old Croats and Serbs in the old Serbo-Croat. It was still a vowel, "jat." Later on, it received different reflexes. The destiny of this cluster "jat" has arrived to distinguish between the Serbian, Croat and Bosniak linguistic areas. There are three basic linguistic reflexes. The long "jat" or the short "jat." The long "jat" in Ekavian reflects as vowel "E", as in the word "dete," d-e-t-e. In Ikavian it is "dite," d-i-t-e, and in Ijekavian it is "dijete," d-i-j-e-t-e. The short "jat" is reflected in Ekavian as a short "E", as in "pesma," p-e-s-m-a. In Ikavian "pisma," p-i-s-m-a and in Ijekavian as "pjesma," p-j-e-s-m-a. These would be the main reflexes. There are Stokavians who use the three, Ijekavian, Ikavian, and Ekavian dialects. There are also Cakavians who use the three dialects or language variants. And let me not belabour the point. There are also transitional speeches, the so-called Ekavian, Ijekavian, Ikavian, Ekavian, but these would be the fundamental differences or reflexes. The biggest problem is the reflex of the long "jat," which reflects into I-J-E, as in "dijete," "blijeda," "bijela." The rule calls for two syllables, but there are also speakers who use just one syllable, like in the western Stokavian dialect. For example, in the Croatian, the literal variant differs from the speech variant. For example, that's how our Mr. Beara speaks when he uses the literary language. At least that's how he spoke in April. I believe that this would be enough about the reflexes of "jat."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree, I agree with that. And if you could help me with the other two sections that we talked about, and that would be the shorter infinitive, which I think you described a little bit, and then the future construction of the western type and the lexical details therefore. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The infinitive, such as to work, to see, to watch, and so on and so forth, in eastern areas of the former common Serbian or Croatian language, would commonly consist of longer "I" sounds, as in "raditi peci," and as you move further towards the western part of the linguistic area, you will encounter the shorter variant more and more often, such as in "radit pec" without the "I" at the end. And when we talk about the future tense, there are two basic models. In the eastern part of the area, which also implies the current, literally, Serbian language of the Ekavian variant, i.e., in Serbia, the most common construction would be "ja cu da radim," "ja cu da dodjen" [phoen]. This construction prevails over the construction with the future tense proper, "ja cu raditi" or "radit cu." And moving towards the west, what dominates the linguistic area is the form "ja cu radit," where the infinitive is shorter, or "radit cu," again with the shorter infinitive. The construction with the word "da," D-A, is something that you will never hear in the western-most parts of this linguistic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I -- if you need to go on, I never want to interrupt, truly, but I think we have the essence of it. And if necessary, you just let me know and I'm sure we'll allow you to continue on. What I'd like to do is to during this -- in this section, Roman numeral VII in your report, you talk about a linguistic cocktail, if you will, and you use the term "recoding" and I know that you describe Mr. Beara's language usage within this section, and I just want to have a better understanding of what you mean by "linguistic cocktail," and then ultimately the recoding, and then the opinion that you have towards the end of that section, Roman numeral VII, which is near Roman numeral VIII, on that last paragraph, and just tell us in essence what is this linguistic cocktail that you referenced?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: As I approached the task at hand, I could observe that in a majority of the transcripts of the allegedly intercepted conversations, what dominates is a correct literary language, which is not marked by any variant features, and one cannot say that it would be marked according to the either eastern or western variant rules. There are no texts for which you could say this is pure Ekavian or this is the eastern variant of the literary language, and the other, in turn, is a pure western variant. Furthermore, I noticed that there are no differences, in terms of dialect, that would point to the region where Mr. Beara was born. Starting from the assumption that transcripts are attributed to his name, I was looking for some characteristics that would point to that, that would lead to such an identification. I was faced with rather scarce material, and let me just note at this point that I entered in the computer, in "Conscripta Continua" [phoen], all the words attributed to Mr. Beara from all the 18 transcripts, and all the 18 of them have been reduced to not more than two and a half pages of computer text, of which more than a half contain absolutely irrelevant words, insignificant words, like "yes," "hello," "okay," "I understand," "I will," "I won't," things like that. And then I sought the and found the starting point for my analysis in the three features or characteristics of the speech, which were "jat," the infinitive and the future tense. I wanted to see what prevails in these three characteristic forms. And as I've already pointed out, that Beara uses words "blijeda" and "ubljedila," which are part of the Croatian literary conversational utterance that you will hear in Split among the interlocutors who used the literary language. This would not be part of the Serbian dialect of the western parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, help us with this, although we didn't give you previously any audio recordings because we were under the mistaken impression that none existed, and then recently we were provided with some audio recordings. And, specifically, what I'd like to direct your attention to is an interview that Mr. Beara was at at the UNDU while he was being questioned by an investigator from the OTP. And just so the record is clear -- the question is a little long because I would like the Court and all of us to be able to follow. This is an interview that occurred shortly after Mr. Beara's arrival here at the Hague on the 11th of October, 2004, and it was a tape that was produced to us for the first time on the 16th of July, 2008. I know that's not relevant for you, but we didn't have that audio recording or transcript prior to July of this year, although the interview was approximately four years ago. Were you able to, over the weekend, with me and others on our team, listen to this audio transcript or audio recording? You don't have to have it before you. We'll go over it a little later. I just want to have it as a foundation. Were you able to listen to it on Saturday or Sunday with us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What we're going to do now, Professor, is look at the methodology that you utilised in analysing the intercepts, those 18 that you were provided. And we'll come back to the audio recording that we just mentioned. So if you turn to section Roman numeral VIII of your report, so we can all follow along and if you need it, you're welcome to that. You identify specifically seven methodological approaches and issues that you wanted to address in performing the analysis and in reaching the opinions that you have in this case, and if you could just highlight them for us, because I do have a question on a couple of them. So what was your methodological approach?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: My methodological approach was based on the assumption that there had to be some traces of the dialect or the mist in which Mr. Beara had grown up, which would be Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor. We didn't hear after you said "dragova" [phoen]. The word wasn't translated for us. You said that there are some traces of the dialect and the "mist," and then we didn't get the second part. If you could just help us with that, and then you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I expected to find traces of the dialect of Beara's youth, which I did not find because they were simply not there, apparently, or at least not in that very limited body of material. There were some differential traces, but there was no possibility to discern the colour of the vowels or accent. I could not check that because there was no opportunity for me to do that, because there was no recording that would show that. Furthermore, I also wanted to see whether, in these transcripts, Mr. Beara introduced himself personally by the first or last name, or whether any of his collocutors identified him. Also, I put transcripts in the context of the variants of the common Serbian and Croatian language, which today are two different literary languages. It has turned out, as you have seen, that when a literary language is in question and when the differential specifics turn up, in his today's speech this is mostly the western variant or today's literary Croatian language. Obviously, I based my conclusions, taking into account a degree of relevance, on the context and the volume of the text. And I also collated the manuscripts and the versions that were subsequently typed up, and I also encountered some discrepancies there. For example, the operator would first record in his hand and then type something by computer, and this is important not in the cases where we have manuscripts, because it is the manuscript that prevails, and the computer typing is irrelevant. Let me repeat, where there is no manuscript or a handwritten version written by the operator, but only a printed version, and to make matters even worse, we don't have manuscripts in those cases where we have most of the texts, so that my conclusions would have been more firmly grounded if there were manuscripts for every conversation and if it were identical to the version that I have been provided with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And thank you for that, and we're looking still at the methodological approach that you utilised, and we said that you highlighted seven of them here in your report on Roman numeral VIII, and then you go on to say that part of your task was indeed to identify the likelihood or the reasonableness of whether or not any of those purported captured, intercepted conversations may be attributed to Mr. Beara; correct? And if you could look at the last paragraph immediately before section 11, you'll find that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Which one, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's at the end of the section Roman numeral VIII, which had the seven methodological factors that you utilised in giving us your approach, and I said that it followed, and it's that paragraph there, that last paragraph, that I was describing or trying to assist us in trying to define specifically what you were tasked to do. And just so the record's clear, the next section obviously should be Roman numeral IX which follows Roman numeral VIII, but as printed, it's identified as Roman numeral XI, so for our purposes, let's just go with the Roman numeral VIII again where you identify the methodological factors that you utilised in your approach, and again my question for you, Professor, is that your task was to identify based on this approach and the materials that you were provided to determine whether or not the purported intercept conversations can be attributed to Mr. Beara based on the linguistics and dialectal information that's provided to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, in page 14 of your report, and I think it goes on to page 15. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I can't see it. I don't know which version you have. What is the heading of that so-called 11th chapter? What is the heading?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's forget about the 11th chapter and let's deal with the 8th chapter, because that's where it's contained. Roman numeral VIII, the caption is: "Analytical Basis for Critical Study of the Manuscripts said to be Connected to Ljubisa Beara," so it's Roman numeral VIII, and I direct your attention, if I may --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- to the last paragraph of that Roman numeral VIII.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: In my version, the chapter VIII is a critical analysis of the text dated from the 13th of July to the 2nd of August, 1995. This is in my version the 8th chapter --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Immediately above that, sir, you have a paragraph and I think it's there I won't go on. Just immediately above that Roman numeral that you've identified, does it talk about the likelihood -- that your task being the likelihood to analyse the text to determine whether or not it may be attributed to Mr. Beara; is that what you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Excellent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll go through each of the intercepts, maybe not in the order that you have it, but I'd like to go -- so I'd like you to concentrate and follow with me. Generally speaking, were you able to formulate an opinion as to whether or not, based upon your review of the materials, knowing the brief background of Mr. Beara, both from his childhood, his military education and military experience, as well from conducting a seven- to eight-hour visit with him, were you able to conclude whether or not any of the intercepts can or may be attributed to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I think I've already said that the language of those 18 transcripts, taken as a whole, in principle, the language -- today's language that Mr. Beara spoke on the 7th and 8th of April, are two incompatible, very different categories or matters. So if we were to depart from his conversational Cakavian-Ikavian Split speech type, which he used when speaking to us those two days, then the content of those transcripts must be rejected a priori, at first hand. In those, I found only one typical word from the Cakavian dialect, which would be differentiating, which never was repeated, but I took as my departure point the reality as well that Mr. Beara, on the 7th and 8th spoke in literary language, there were parts or whole sentences spoken in literary language, and on these occasions the variant used was that of the Croatian literary language, a Zagreb variant of the one-time common language, and then I allowed for the possibility that the transcripts, in which there are several or multiple features -- characters of details of that variant, of that type of language, these may be connected to Mr. Beara. With respect to one transcript, I decidedly, although with not a high degree of reliability and certainty, I characterized it that it may be accepted that it may be attributed to Beara, and this is the one on the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and we'll get to that, actually, now. Before we do that, when we talk about your methodological approach, you also did this analysis, and I just want to direct your attention, as well as my learned friends' and the Court, to table -- or annex 1 of your report, which is a table that you created of those 18 intercepts, and you have basically four questions that you've identified there, whether -- as you identified in your methodology, whether the person compromised himself or revealed himself or was compromised by the other speaker, and then you go on and have three other categories: Is the -- or does the dialect clearly identify the speaker's origin, is the dialect tied to the person's region, and, finally, is the speaker's dialect close to Ljubisa Beara's current manner of speech. Do you have that table annex 1 in front of you of your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that everyone's following along -- thank you. So that everyone's following along, it is 2D551. And in that report, sir, you identified conversations that you reviewed with these four questions, now just -- although you've provided us with a brief explanation of what the symbols, the hyphen, the zero and the positive sign indicate, can you tell us exactly, so that we understand it, what do you mean when you use the symbol "O" or zero?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: This means no data, no data.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then the negative sign or the minus sign, if you will?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: A negative sign denotes that he did not introduce himself. When we say zero, this means that it doesn't refer to Beara, some other people are referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the positive or the plus sign or symbol that you utilised, what does it indicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: This is confirmation. This is a response in the affirmative, whether he was revealed or -- himself or by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, but really those symbols that you use, the negative, the positive, as well as the zero symbols, you use that for four independent questions that you provide in your table, so it isn't just whether Mr. Beara compromised or revealed his identity, or whether another person purportedly speaking with him compromised his identity. You used those symbols for all four categories, including the fourth category which is whether, essentially, the speaker's dialect was close or consistent with Ljubisa Beara's current speech pattern or manner of speech; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I use those symbols on the basis of the general image, the general impression. When I took into account all the elements that were available to me, when they were tangible to me to be analysed. This is a synthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I'm trying as well as to try to synthesize as briefly as possible. And now you were just mentioning to us that with respect to the August 1st, 1995, intercept, although you didn't mention the time, we can look at this table and we see within those four categories that you actually have a positive or plus sign, and the time of this intercept is exactly --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Early morning, yes. That's 10.02 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Take a look at your table. Do you have your table, by -- and look on the left column, where it says "1 August, 10002." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we draw across this column and we see that you have four positive symbols, and you've answered "positive" or "yes" to the four questions that you identify in the top section of this table, which is essentially your brief overview and analysis of the results of the intercepts that you reviewed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the 1st of August, 1002 intercept analysis that you conducted, and you'll find that in your next section of your report, and why don't we start there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're way quicker than I am, and I appreciate that. Now, within this intercept, can you identify for us -- and so that the Court will have it, we ask that it be brought up in e-court; and it's specifically P1378B for the B/C/S and P1378A for the English version. And, sir, you have that, and you should hopefully have that in front of you as well. I know you have the analysis in front of you. I don't know if you need the actual transcript that was provided in connection with this purported intercept. Can you share with us what your conclusion is in connection with this August 1st, 1995 intercept at 1002 hundred hours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: As per the allegations of the operator, Mr. Beara introduced himself: "Hello, good day, Ljubisa Beara speaking." This was done by his collocutor. He mentioned his name. The linguistic corpus or the body of the language is not very rich, but it does not collide or it's not very opposite in terms of the identification stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that we could follow along, Professor Remetic, and I promise I'm not interrupting you to shorten your testimony, and if we could just turn to the second page of the English version where I think the professor is focusing on Mr. Beara identifying himself, just so we could all follow along, if the Court doesn't mind. Go ahead, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This text, the same as others, does not contain variants where literary language would be marked by a variant. There are details, features, characteristics of the western variant or the Croatian literary language, but there are also those which resemble the eastern variant. I opted to give precedence to those which carry more weight, and therefore I attributed more importance to the examples of the western variant. For me, "izvjestio" with an I-G-E, "to report" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where are you finding that in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: In the transcript? In the manuscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: So "izvjestio," "report," then the truncated form of the infinitive, like in "pozvat," "to call," or "dogovorit," "to arrange," but also "naci," "to find," there is an elongated -- a full version of the infinitive. In the transcripts, what is often found is the noun "burazer" or "brother," which is not limited in terms of linguistic variance but is more frequent in the west than it is in the east. And here what is used is the shorter version, "buraz," which is more often found in the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're trying to follow along, and I know this is like a two-part conversation, and I think if we look, it's the fourth line of the conversation that introduces Mr. Beara, correct, where you're speaking now of the "buraz," which is the short form of "burazer"; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now please continue with your analysis of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Here, there are infinitives following the western variant, such as "Hoces li biti u firmi," which means "will you be at the company," and next to a construction which is typical of the eastern variant, "ja cu da dodjem," the eastern variant of the future tense formation. Let me explain my conclusions. I allowed for the possibility, and my conscience is telling me to allow for this possibility, that this could be Beara speaking, that this could be Beara's speech type, because even today he would say "izvjestio" with an I-G-E, or also say "izvjestija," as in the Ikavian. Then he would say "pozvat" [phoen], and I heard him speak, "buraz" as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's why, Professor, you identified in your table the four questions as all being positive; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Just in the interests of time, and I know that you've spent an inordinate amount of time analysing these intercepts, and we all are grateful for that, but we do have to move on a little bit. If there's something however that you feel is necessary to add, I will allow you and I'm sure the court will insist that you provide us with that further analysis or discussion. What I want to do is to look at the next intercept which was also dated the 1st of August, and we have two times recorded in your table of 2245 and 2308, and that is the -- I'm sorry, I may have misspoken. The next one we want is 65 ter P1395, which is an intercept that is -- no, let's go with the one -- I'm sorry again, I apologise. I lost my spot, and I apologise to the Court. We need Exhibit P1380, please, and that is the intercept from the 1st of August, 1995, at 2245. Again, I think the witness is just asking for clarification. I'll just restate it, I think, for his benefit. Professor, if you look at your table --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Everything's in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Great. And then we'll get that up on the screen. You've also analysed and reviewed this intercept of 2245. You include within it another section which is identified as -- by the time 2308. Can you tell me, why is that? Maybe I can help, because I don't think it's a big secret. That intercept actually is contained in two pages, which is P1380B, and the second page of that intercept has another intercept below it which designates the time as 2308. The beginning of this P1380B has the time as you've identified it as 2245. So it's really two pages, and I think that's -- or tell us why you included both those times there. And you treated it as one, I believe.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I treated those as a single conversation. It continues, as you can see. There is quite a lengthy conversation, the first one, and then there is a very short intervening time, and there were other circumstances which connect them. This is a long text, two relatively long texts for which there are no manuscripts. There is nothing written in handwriting by the operator. I did not receive it, anyway, or at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's true also for the prior intercept, the 1st of August at 1002 hundred hours, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: At 10.00, I believe this holds for that as well. There's no manuscript for that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The 1st of August is without manuscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say "manuscript," you're saying there's no handwritten capturing of the conversation --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: "Manuscript" is something written in longhand, the operator's handwritten version, or whoever wrote those things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, focusing back on this second intercept that we're looking at of the 1st of August at 2245 and 2308, tell us what your analysis found in connection with this intercept.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: You see, the language of these conversations is incompatible with the language of the morning conversation from 1002.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I understand you, but let me try to say this: Are you saying that the conversations are incompatible because it cannot be the same person? If we assume that the conversation at 1002 is Mr. Beara, it certainly cannot be Mr. Beara at 2245 and 2308? Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object, and that is completely leading. I think there's a much more reasonable way to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It couldn't be more leading than that actually, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "incompatible," sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: That means something which cannot be connected, something completely different, something opposite. In the texts, allegedly recorded conversations in the evening, we have domination of Ekavian variant. We have Ekavian speech, like "mesto," "odseku," "covek;" only two forms in the Ijekavian, like "razumijem" and "dvije." Mr. Beara speaks only "razumim," and this is the word he used in the conversation with the Prosecutor in October, and this is what we are going to see further on. Furthermore, I tried to explain away these Ekavian occurrences by possible adaptations to the manner of -- the manner of speech of the collocutor. However, his collocutor uses more Ijekavian words than Ekavian. Furthermore, we have a truncated infinitive together with Ekavian forms, which is illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And which we didn't see in the prior intercept, or have we seen it in the prior intercept of 1002 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did we find that in the prior intercept or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: There was not so much Ekavian in there. Please, this is Ekavian. Here, there are 15 Ekavian words that are written down, printed; not in the manuscript, though, mind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I think we need 25 minutes to be able to digest all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Twenty-five minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, if I may ask you, are you okay to proceed? I know it's been long and you've done a lot of talking and testifying here today. Are you physically okay and can we proceed for another 40 or so minutes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The break was long enough. As far as I am concerned, we can go on until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Great, thank you. I don't think it will be necessary, however. Sir, we were discussing the 2nd of August intercept at specifically the 2245 and 2308 hundred hours, and looking at your table, I note that you have, obviously, minus or negative signs on the four columns which you used to analyse the transcripts, and I recognise also you told us that for this intercept, among others, such as the 1st of August at 1002, there was no manuscript. With respect to this specific intercept that we're looking at, the 1st of August, 2245 and 2308, were you able to reach a conclusion or an opinion, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, as to whether or not these intercepts may be attributed to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: According to my experience in my profession, and the familiarity with the circumstances in the Serbian and Croatian linguistic area, one person cannot utter, within one day or within 13 or so hours, the speeches that differ to such an extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I know --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The language on the 1st of August, in these three -- or, rather, two conversations, is a mixture which cannot be put together in any natural way. The afternoon conversation cannot be, in my opinion, linked with the name of Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And let me focus, if I may, on the use of the first column that you had, which says whether there was a compromise of the identity by either the speaker or the person with whom he was speaking to, and you have a negative sign in that section. If we look at the body of the text, which is again, just for the record, P1380B, the B/C/S version, and the English version would be P1380A, we note that in the body of the text there, I think according to your table, there is no reference to anyone identifying or compromising the identity of an individual such as Mr. Beara. However, in the beginning part of that text, in the introduction part, which doesn't capture the conversation, someone identifies him as Mr. Beara. Do you know how that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Also speculation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's a reasonable question, given the evidence that's been presented. It's certainly factual specifically as to what I said, and if he can deduct -- and it really goes more to his table, why he didn't put a plus or a zero as opposed to a negative there. So I'm really leading him or trying to obtain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but is the professor the ideal person to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not the ideal person, obviously. If you'd like, I can move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can he explain what -- whoever jotted that down that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, in looking at this, did you find more instances where, in the body of the text of an intercept, references were made to the name "Ljubo" or the word "Ljubo," or a derivative of that word, and did you find as to whether or not the Prosecution has taken a position that it's an unknown individual? In other intercepts that you may have reviewed, did you see that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand your question. Are we talking about this person Stevo here who uses the word "Ljubo," and nobody introduces themselves as Ljubo Beara? That's what you can find in my table, nobody introduces themselves as Ljubo Beara. And "Ljubo" can refer to a host of names, a host of people, if you just used a "Ljubo."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that a little later, hopefully. Let's look at the next intercept which is P1395, and we have the intercept of the 2nd of August at 1300 hours. And I'd like to just highlight a couple of things in this intercept, and if I'm allowed, it would be P1305D, as in "dog" for the record, and then it would be P1395C in the English version, and then D would have been the manuscript handwritten version and P1395D is the typed manuscript. And then we have another one related to that, which was I think the translation of the manuscript, which is P1395F, as in "Frank," just so the Court has the full complete set of this intercept. So, sir, I'm directing your attention to the 2nd of August 19995 at 1300 hours, which is a collection of an intercept, and did you have an opportunity to review this intercept as well? I think it's the very next one in your table, so second from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about the conversation which took place on the 2nd of August at 1300 hours, this conversation was practically irrelevant for my job, because there's no text, there are no words in there which may be linked with the name of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing, please, please. But the text is important for another reason or another fact. The person who typed it on the computer, the typist, obviously did not make a distinction between the reflexes found in the Jekavian and Ijekavian of the "jat" cluster. When he copied the text from the manuscript, which in my view was correct, he copied the features "izvjestaj" [phoen] or "report," "covjeca" [phoen] or "man," and typed them in a way that nobody, as far as I know, would actually use them in speech. His copy reads "izvjestaj" and "cavijece" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, let me catch up with you, and the rest of us. And I think the record noted on page 65 that it was P1905 that we were calling up, but it's actually P1395 and the collection therefrom. And I'd like if we could have on the screen the "D", which is the written manuscript, again P1395D, and then immediately thereafter we're going to go to the typed script, which is P1395B. And just show us where that word appears, Professor, if you don't mind, at this August 2nd, 1995, 1300 hour intercept. And if possible, Mr. President, would the usher be able to provide him with a pen, and then maybe he can highlight it or underline it for us, or circle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Professor, they have a special pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Shall I put circles around things or shall I underline them? What do you want me to do? "Izvjestija" [phoen] here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, I think what we need on the left-hand side of the screen so you can see it --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: In the manuscript, it is transcribed correctly. The way the word is spelled in the manuscript is good. I'm just looking now for the word "covjeca" or "man."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Hold on, please, Professor. Professor, that is on the next page, but I will turn to the next page when I am done looking at this. Right now, I would like us to have the typed B/C/S version of this handwritten manuscript, which I have with the ERN number 0108-5009, which again my understanding is P1395B, as in "boy," so that we could then circle it also in the typed version and then get a better appreciation for that which is what you're trying to convey to us here. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Where is the typed version, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They're trying to get it for us now. We can possibly, because it's just one word, have him just recircle it, if we have both up, whichever the Court's pleasure is. I had noticed that the left side was the English version, but we need the typewritten B/C/S and then the handwritten B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think we need to save it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They'll bring it up, Professor, in a couple of seconds. Just be patient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll bear with you as long as it takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can just scroll it down --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a little, and at the bottom of that -- there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, can you also circle the word which is the typed version of the same word that you circled in the handwritten version, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that we can better have an appreciation --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: And "covijece" [phoen] is a bit further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's actually on the next page of both the manuscript and the typed text, but let's stay with this for a second. You noted that this word from the manuscript handwritten text was typed differently than that which it appeared on the typewritten text; is that what you're trying to share with us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is that why --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes, please. In the manuscript, in the handwritten version, everything is okay, both "covijece" and "izvjestija." In the typed version, we find a hyper Ijekavian version. It has been copied erroneously, and in my view this is a serious mistake because it throws a different light on the text where there is no manuscript, where manuscripts are missing, where there's only a typed version, thus unabling [as interpreted] us to check the credibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: -- of the both texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, with the Court's permission, if we could turn to the second page of both documents, and again if -- first we should probably save the circled typed version, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's been suggested to us that for practical reasons, your witness should also circle the relative word in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could direct him to do that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you could once again circle the word that we're discussing here on the handwritten manuscript which then corresponds or correlates with the typewritten one on the left of the screen. So can you do that for us, please, again? In the handwritten text, if you could circle the word we were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt. I noticed in the transcript that the witness had indicated that the difference between the transcription and the handwriting changes the meaning, and it was unclear to me whether he meant to refer to the meaning of the word or the meaning of the word in terms of its ability to -- linguistically, in order to identify a person, and I wonder if my good friend could clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As soon as we get there, I will most certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you circle the word again, "izvjestaj" in the handwritten portion? Can you take the pen and circle again in the handwritten text where that word appears?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Now, sir, when you look at these two words, and I think in the record it may have reflected, as my learned friend said, that it changes or alters the meaning of the word, can you just again describe for us what effect, in your opinion, professionally speaking, does the difference in adding an "I" on the typed text, versus the handwritten text, which doesn't have an "I", does it change the meaning of the word or does it to you, as a linguistics expert and professor of dialectology, does it indicate for you any specific characteristics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The focus here is on the issue of the reliability or the lack thereof of these people who actually typed these texts. These two forms indicate that they were not reliable, that they were not enclitic enough, and this shows that there may be mistakes in the other texts as well, but these cannot be collated against manuscripts. When it comes to the semantics, the words "lepo" and "lijepo" do not differ in semantic terms, they mean the same, but they are used in different areas, in different parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From that, you can detect which region or area someone is from, correct, or at least reasonably conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the "jat"s reflexes, reflections, you can guess where a person comes from, but in this case they wrote down the form of the word that nobody speaks anywhere, the "izvjestaj" and "covijece." We haven't registered such forms, which testifies to the degree of the reliability of the typists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so we have a complete record with respect to this intercept, if we can please save this, and we'll identify it accordingly tonight and tomorrow, and then I would ask that we go to the second page of both documents, with the Court's permission, if we can save this. Now, Professor, in front of you, you should have the second page of this intercept of the 2nd of August at 1300 hours, and can you go through the same exercise, with the assistance of the usher, and circle the word which you were focusing on and that which you referred to in your report where there was a change from what was written, in your view, linguistically and dialectically having an impact? And I think the word is "covijece," as you earlier referenced, and now we can find it and if you could be kind enough to circle it both on the handwritten and the typed texts. You're going to have to use a special --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: The word "covijece" in the manuscript, here it is, "covijece" or "man" [marks]. This text is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you look at the fourth line --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Here it is, here it is, here it is. Okay. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we can also save this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, again, with respect to this word, you also find that this -- what's the significance of the difference in the handwritten versus the typed text? How is that significant to you in your analysis and the opinions that you're providing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, those mistakes undermine the authority, they compromise the authority of the typists, so we must be cautious when we read the manuscripts or texts which do not exist in the longhand version. I'm not sure to which degree these texts are reliable. This is a corpus delicti.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, and we only have ten or so minutes left, and I want to ask you -- there's another intercept there, and we'll go through that exercise hopefully today or tomorrow. What I want to know now, looking at your table, I note there are certain entries with the time periods of the intercepts. Are you able to conclude as to looking at your positive signs, from the 16th of July, namely at 1111 hours, all the way through to the 1st of August at 1002, can you tell us as to whether or not there were any intercepts that were captured that purport to be attributed to Mr. Beara during the time period, again, from the 16th of July through the 1st of August at 1002 hundred hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question is vague as to what intercepts my colleague is talking about, whether these are intercepts he reviewed, or intercepts he was provided with, or intercepts in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously the intercepts that he reviewed. If there are other intercepts, we'd be more than happy to have them, but we don't have any others in our possession in connection with anything purportedly attributing to Mr. Beara for that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you help us with that? Did you find, of the intercepts that you reviewed, any intercepts that purport or can be attributed to Mr. Beara from the time period of the 16th of July through the 1st of August? And I just note, if we look at your table, you obviously have a positive sign on the 16th of July and you have a positive sign on the 1st of August, so my question is: For that two or so-week period, did you find any evidence of any such intercepts that would be attributed to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't found any.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Within that time period, though, we see two other intercepts; specifically, the 23rd of July, 1995, at 0805 hours, and I think it's 65 ter 1310. Now, in that intercept, although it was given to you as a collection of references or possibly intercepts that bear the name of Beara or the name Ljubo, I'd like to focus, in the brief time that we have, specifically on this intercept the 23rd of July, 0805 hours, and again the 65 ter number is 1310. And just see we have a clean --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Which date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 23. And just so the record is clear, Mr. President, we're going to call up P1310B, as in "boy," which is the B/C/S version, and I think also P1310C, which I believe may be the typed version, and the English version is P1310A. So we would only need the "B" and the "A" version of the intercept on the screen for these limited questions. You let me know, Professor, when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this intercepts, we have a few minutes left, with respect to this intercept, you have identified in your report circles or the zero symbol in the four sections in the questions that you raised. Now, did we -- and it says in your report, but you reviewed also the Prosecution's position, just again so that they have it, from the 1st of May, 2007, as to who the Ljubo in this intercept is, but I'm asking you: Were you advised as to who the Ljubo was in the intercept that purports to be the 23rd of July, 1995, at 0805 hours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Please, much earlier I had prepared an analysis, and in my report it is stated that it is unclear which Ljubo is being referred to. There are no indications pointing to Mr. Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: And, anyway, the Prosecution -- the Prosecution means -- think that this refers to Major Ljubo Bojanovic, so this has nothing to do with Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Court has that filing from the 1st of May, 2007, and if they look plainly on page 73, they'll find the intercept and they'll find the OTP's position that it's Ljubo Bojanovic, so I just want to clarify that, because we're talking about the period from the 16th of July to August 1st. Similarly, in the three minutes that we have left, let's take a look at the next intercept which is dated the 25th of July, which is at 0709 hours, which for all of us following it would be P1328B, as in "boy," and P1328A, as in "apple." Can we go to that next intercept, Professor, of the 25th of July at 0709 hours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC
utterances.text: Here, too, it is unclear which Ljubo is being referred to. This material is extremely meager. There are several soldierly, terse questions and answers, greetings like "hello," "excellent," "okay," "well," "very well." Two times "gide" [phoen] occurs, which contrasts today's Beara's manner of speech, and, anyway, the Prosecution, concurring with me, thinks that it is not clear which Ljubo is being referred to. Not even the Prosecutors think that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's stop there for today. We will proceed with your testimony tomorrow, Professor. Have a good rest, and we'll reconvene tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
